title: Kenyan primary-care LLM produced actively harmful clinical recommendations
ai_system_or_tool: AI Consult / OpenAI-backed large language model
summary: A retrospective physician review of 1,469 encounters from an EHR-embedded LLM clinical decision-support system deployed across 16 Kenyan primary-care clinics between July and September 2024 identified 115 encounters (7.8%) containing actively harmful LLM recommendations. Sixty-seven harmful recommendations appeared in final clinical documentation. The study also found 50 hallucination encounters and reported that inappropriate advice could include tests unavailable locally or medicines outside local formularies. This record documents unsafe model outputs and their adoption in documentation; it does not infer patient injury where the study did not establish it.
response: The peer-reviewed evaluation recommended usability optimisation, local guardrails and prospective trials. A later cluster-randomised trial reported no serious adverse events judged related to the intervention and no statistically significant reduction in 14-day treatment failure.
regulatory_or_legal_outcome: No regulatory or legal outcome identified in reviewed sources.
qualification_basis: Peer-reviewed Nature Health study directly evaluated a deployed Kenyan clinical system and quantified actively harmful recommendations; PubMed independently indexes the same study. The record carefully distinguishes unsafe recommendations from proven patient-level injury.
source_1_name: Nature Health - Safety of a large language model-based clinical decision support system in African primary healthcare
notes: Incident date is month-level because the evaluated deployment window ran July-September 2024. The later 2025 pragmatic trial is contextual evidence and should not be misread as invalidating the documented unsafe outputs in the earlier evaluation.

title: South African lawyers relied on ChatGPT-generated fictitious legal authorities
sector: Legal services and administration of justice
summary: In Parker v Forsyth NNO and Others, the plaintiff's legal team relied on legal research sourced through ChatGPT. The cited authorities could not be located and the attorneys ultimately admitted they had not accessed or read them. The court described the lawyers as placing undue faith in AI-generated legal research and failing to verify it. This is a documented professional-use failure rather than a synthetic-media incident.
response: The false authorities were challenged and the court criticised the failure to verify AI-generated legal research. The case subsequently became a reference point in South African judicial discussion of professional AI use.
regulatory_or_legal_outcome: The underlying action was dismissed with costs; reviewed judicial materials use the episode as a warning about professional verification duties.
qualification_basis: The AI linkage is directly documented in South African judicial material: the cited cases were sourced from ChatGPT and could not be verified. Later High Court authority in Mavundla reproduces and discusses the Parker episode.
source_1_name: LawLibrary - Parker v Forsyth NNO and Others [2023] ZAGPRD 1
notes: AAIO does not attribute every adverse outcome in the litigation to ChatGPT. The incident recorded is the production and professional reliance on fictitious AI-generated authorities and the resulting verification/court-process burden.
